title: What may be sung
hook: only Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal are sung in kirtan

segments.voice: Yesterday, prakash and sukhasan: the Granth opened in light at dawn, rested with care at night. Your line was open and rest. What did you put down gently last night? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

A harmonium wheezes into its first chord. A tabla player taps the skin twice to check the pitch. Three singers sit cross-legged on a low platform to the side of the Granth, and the hall goes quiet the way a hall does when music is about to start. In that moment, a question has already been answered, long before anyone sat down. Not which tune. Not which instrument. Which words. The code is strict about it, and the strictness tells you something about what a sung line can do to a person.
screen: `A HARMONIUM'S FIRST CHORD.` → `THE HALL GOES QUIET.` → `NOT WHICH TUNE. WHICH WORDS.`

segments.voice: The singing is called kirtan, the sung praise of God. In paraphrase, the code says that in the sangat, kirtan is to be only of Gurbani, the Gurus' own words, or of the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal, which explain Gurbani. That's the whole list. A gifted singer doesn't perform a hymn they wrote last week, however moving it is. A famous poem doesn't get in because it's beautiful. Why draw the line so tight? Go back to the sangat. Guru Nanak said the true company is known by what is said there. A melody is glue for words. A tune can carry a line long after the page is closed. Whatever is sung in the hall is what the sangat will hum in the kitchen, on the drive home, at the hospital bed. So the code guards the words, because the words are what the music will plant. Now look at the two names on the list. Bhai Gurdas was a Sikh scholar and poet close to the Gurus; tradition calls his writing a key to Gurbani. Bhai Nand Lal was a poet in the Tenth Guru's court, the one we met with the poets of Anandpur. Neither is a Guru. Their works are allowed as explanation. So even the exceptions point back to the Guru's word. This is a rule for kirtan in the sangat. It isn't a rule that Sikhs never write or sing anything else. Poetry, folk songs and new music all have their places in Sikh life. But in the hall, in front of the Granth, the voice belongs to the Guru. Only the word.
screen: `KIRTAN: THE SUNG PRAISE OF GOD.` · `ONLY GURBANI, AND TWO WHO EXPLAIN IT.` · `A MELODY PLANTS THE WORDS.` · `A RULE FOR THE HALL.` · then, large: `ONLY THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for which words are sung. Settle, and breathe. Bring up a song that's been stuck in your head lately. Don't judge it. Just say its words slowly, without the tune. What do they actually say? Would you choose to repeat them to yourself all day, if you'd chosen on purpose? If you know a line of Gurbani or a line from any text you love, let it play instead, quietly, and notice how it sits. Rest with that until the bell. The bell holds the time.
What may be sung. In the sangat, kirtan is only Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal, which explain it. Today's word.
Your line: only the word. Today, notice the words of every song you hear, and keep the one line worth humming all day. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara, ragis sing kirtan from Gurbani, sometimes with the works of Bhai Gurdas or Bhai Nand Lal, usually with harmonium and tabla; the words are often shown on a screen for the sangat to follow.
